F1-01.name: Cart-mandate tampering via indirect prompt injection
F1-01.actor: An operator who controls third-party content a shopping agent reads — a marketplace listing, a review block, a comparison page. No access to the issuer, the customer's device, or the mandate signing key is required, which is precisely what makes this cheap.
F1-01.genai_enabler: The agent cannot reliably separate retrieved content from instructions, so text placed in a product description is processed as direction rather than data. GenAI also makes the payload itself disposable: injection strings can be generated, varied and A/B-tested against agent behaviour at negligible cost.
F1-01.description: The human issues a cart mandate over a basket they reviewed. Between mandate issuance and authorisation the agent ingests attacker-influenced content, which steers it into substituting a merchant, adding a line item, or raising the amount. The authorisation that reaches the issuer is cryptographically well-formed and carries a genuine consent signature — the human really did consent, just not to this basket. The gap between the signed intent and the settled purchase is the whole attack, and the provenance chain is where that gap becomes visible.
preconditions: Agent operates under a cart mandate whose scope was fixed before the final basket was assembled.
Agent ingests untrusted third-party content between mandate issuance and authorisation.
Basket contents are not re-confirmed with the human after that ingestion.

observable_signals.signal: Authorised merchant or MCC is absent from the mandate scope the human agreed to.
Settled amount exceeds the cart ceiling the human saw, usually by a modest margin chosen to stay under review thresholds.
Provenance chain contains a domain never before seen for this customer, ingested immediately before the scope excursion.
Ingested content carries imperative, agent-directed language — instruction-shaped text where a product description should be.
Deliberation collapses; the agent commits with far less reasoning latency than a comparable legitimate purchase of the same size.

mitigations: Bind the mandate hash to the final basket and re-verify the binding at authorisation time.
Treat all retrieved content as data — strip or quarantine instruction-shaped text before it reaches the planner.
Require explicit human re-confirmation whenever the basket changes after content ingestion.
Enforce merchant allow-lists at the network rather than inside the agent, so a compromised planner cannot widen its own scope.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM01 Prompt Injection: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/
Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - cart mandate construction
Mastercard Agent Pay - agentic commerce programme announcement (2025)

F1-02.name: Intent-mandate scope inflation
F1-02.actor: Anyone able to influence the agent's planning context — a compromised or adversarial sub-agent, a poisoned tool result, or a merchant-side content operator. Also reachable by a careless-but-benign agent, which is why the detector must score behaviour rather than intent.
F1-02.genai_enabler: Intent mandates delegate a goal, not a basket, so the agent is granted interpretive latitude by design. An LLM planner can rationalise almost any purchase as serving the stated goal, and can produce a fluent justification for it, which defeats review processes that read the agent's explanation rather than its behaviour.
F1-02.description: A human delegates a goal under an intent mandate with a scope envelope — categories, a maximum amount, a merchant allow-list, a TTL. The agent then transacts outside that envelope: adjacent-category drift ("travel insurance" billed against a flights mandate), amount inflation just under the ceiling followed by a step over it, or substitution of a merchant outside the allow-list. Because the mandate is real and unexpired, everything except the scope check passes. This is the highest-frequency F1 vector precisely because it needs no cryptographic failure — only latitude.
preconditions: Mandate is of type intent, delegating a goal rather than a fixed basket.
Mandate scope carries at least one enforceable constraint (category, amount, merchant, item count).
Scope is enforced advisorily by the agent rather than authoritatively at the network.

observable_signals.signal: Authorised MCC falls outside the categories named in the mandate scope.
Merchant is absent from a non-empty allow-list on the mandate.
Amount sits at or above the scope ceiling, often clustered just beneath it across a campaign.
Basket carries more line items than max_items permits.
The agent's overall spend pattern under one mandate drifts away from the population of agents holding comparable mandates.

mitigations: Enforce mandate scope at the network, not in the agent — the constrained party must not be the enforcing party.
Express category scope as an explicit MCC set rather than natural language, so "adjacent" has no room to mean anything.
Decrement a cumulative budget across the mandate lifetime, not just per transaction, to defeat salami inflation.
Require re-consent when the agent's plan leaves the originally scoped category.
references: Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - intent mandate scope semantics
Mastercard Agent Pay - agent authorisation and consent model (2025)

F1-03.name: Refund-logic hijack
F1-03.actor: An attacker who can place content in front of either the buyer's agent or a merchant-side support agent — a returns page, a support-ticket body, an order note — and who controls a receiving instrument.
F1-03.genai_enabler: Merchants are automating returns and disputes with LLM agents that hold real authority to issue credits. Those agents read attacker-supplied free text as part of their normal job, which makes the refund path the single highest-value instruction-following surface in commerce: it moves money outward, and it is the one flow designed to be generous.
F1-03.description: The attacker manipulates the refund path rather than the purchase path. Two common shapes: the buyer's agent is steered into requesting a refund routed to an instrument other than the one that paid, or a merchant-side support agent is instructed by ticket content to approve a credit that no purchase justifies. Both produce a credit whose destination or magnitude has no matching authorisation history. Refund flows are chronically under-monitored relative to purchase flows, so the same anomaly that would be obvious on a purchase can pass unexamined here.
preconditions: An agent holds authority to initiate or approve refunds or credits.
Refund destination is not hard-bound to the original payment credential.
Free-text content from an untrusted party reaches the agent making the decision.

observable_signals.signal: Credit is routed to an instrument or beneficiary that differs from the one on the original authorisation.
Refund value over a window exceeds prior purchase value for the same customer-merchant pair.
Beneficiary receiving the credit has no prior relationship with this customer.
Ingested ticket or returns content contains directive language aimed at the agent's approval logic rather than at a human reader.
One beneficiary accumulates credits from many unrelated customers or merchants.

mitigations: Hard-bind refunds to the original payment credential; make an alternate destination a separate, human-authorised flow.
Cap agent refund authority by amount and rate, with escalation above the cap.
Require a matching authorisation record before any agent-initiated credit clears.
Score refund flows with the same firewall the purchase flow gets, not a lighter one.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM01 Prompt Injection, excessive agency
Card scheme chargeback and credit-routing rules (refund-to-original-credential principle)

F1-04.name: Intent-mandate category drift
F1-04.actor: An operator who can influence what a shopping agent considers "equivalent" to the goods the human asked for, either through content the agent reads or through a merchant that presents itself under a neighbouring category.
F1-04.genai_enabler: An intent mandate delegates a goal rather than a basket, and the agent must interpret category boundaries in natural language. "Household essentials" admits a reading that includes consumer electronics, and a model can be argued into that reading far more cheaply than a rules engine can.
F1-04.description: The human authorises spend within a set of categories. The agent settles in a category just outside that set, on a merchant whose acceptance code is adjacent to the permitted ones. Every individual step is defensible, the amount is within the ceiling, and the mandate is unexpired; only the category is wrong. Drift is a lower-yield attack than outright substitution, which is precisely why it survives review.
preconditions: An intent mandate whose scope is expressed as categories rather than merchants.
Agent has discretion over merchant selection at authorisation time.
No network-side enforcement of the category list.

observable_signals.signal: The settled MCC is absent from the category list the mandate carried.
The settled category is one the customer has never transacted in before.
Settled category sits far from the permitted set in co-purchase space, not adjacent to it.
The combination of mandate type, category and merchant is rare across the whole population.

mitigations: Enforce the category list at the network, not inside the agent that can reinterpret it.
Express intent scopes as explicit code lists rather than natural-language descriptions.
Re-confirm with the human whenever the settled category is outside the authorised set.
references: Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - intent mandate semantics
ISO 18245 - merchant category code assignment

F1-05.name: Delegation-chain laundering through sub-agents
F1-05.actor: An operator who controls a sub-agent that a primary agent is willing to delegate to - a specialist "booking" or "checkout" capability the primary agent can call at runtime.
F1-05.genai_enabler: Multi-agent orchestration makes delegation cheap and routine, and each hop strips context. By the time the payment is made, the executing agent holds the authority the human granted but none of the constraints the human stated, because those constraints were prose in a planning context two hops back.
F1-05.description: The human delegates to an agent they chose. That agent delegates onward, and the sub-agent transacts. The authorisation carries the human's mandate and a delegation depth the human never contemplated. Authority has been laundered through the chain: the payment is formally authorised and substantively unsupervised. Blast radius grows with every hop, which is why delegation depth is carried explicitly in the schema rather than inferred after the fact.
preconditions: Agent platform permits onward delegation without re-consent.
Mandate does not pin a maximum delegation depth.
Sub-agent identity is not separately registered or attested.

observable_signals.signal: Delegation depth exceeds the maximum the mandate or issuer policy permits.
One agent identifier transacts for an implausible number of distinct customers.
The executing agent runs on a platform this customer has never used.
A single mandate hash appears across agents that share no legitimate relationship.

mitigations: Pin a maximum delegation depth inside the mandate and enforce it at the network.
Require each hop to attest its own identity, so the chain is auditable end to end.
Re-verify consent whenever the executing agent differs from the agent the human chose.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM06 Excessive Agency
Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - delegation and mandate chaining

F1-06.name: Consent-signature stripping and authentication downgrade
F1-06.actor: An operator positioned between the agent and the acquirer, or one able to drive an agent toward a checkout path that accepts weaker evidence of consent.
F1-06.genai_enabler: Agents negotiate checkout paths dynamically and optimise for completion. An agent that treats "the payment succeeded" as its goal will retry down a weaker path when the strong one fails, and can be nudged into doing so by content that frames the weak path as the supported one.
F1-06.description: A purchase that should have carried a verified consent signature is presented without one, or with one that does not verify, on a rail that accepts it anyway. The economic effect is a liability shift: the transaction settles with the customer's credential but without the cryptographic evidence that the customer agreed. Detection matters more than prevention here, because the downgrade usually happens at a party the issuer does not control.
preconditions: A checkout path exists that accepts an agentic purchase with weak or absent consent evidence.
Signature verification failures are treated as soft declines rather than hard stops.

observable_signals.signal: Consent signature is absent or fails cryptographic verification.
Entry mode is weaker than this customer and merchant pair normally uses.
Step-up authentication is skipped on a transaction whose size normally triggers it.
The session's overall shape sits far from the agentic population it claims to belong to.

mitigations: Treat a failed consent-signature verification as a hard decline on the agentic rail.
Refuse silent fallback from a strong checkout path to a weaker one within a session.
Bind the liability model to the verification result, never to the claimed one.
references: EMV 3-D Secure - protocol specification and exemption handling
Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - consent signature verification

F1-07.name: Time-of-check to time-of-use mandate mutation
F1-07.actor: An operator able to influence the agent's state in the window between the human approving a basket and the authorisation reaching the network.
F1-07.genai_enabler: The gap between approval and settlement used to be milliseconds inside a single checkout page. With an agent it can be minutes, spanning tool calls, retries and fresh content retrieval - a mutable window that did not previously exist to be attacked.
F1-07.description: The human reviews and approves. The agent then does more work: re-checking stock, re-pricing, re-reading a listing. Something in that work changes the basket, and the transaction that settles is not the one that was approved. The mandate hash still refers to the approved basket, so the binding between the signed artefact and the settled purchase is where the discrepancy becomes visible. This differs from F1-01 in mechanism rather than effect: no injected instruction is needed, only a mutable window and a race.
preconditions: A non-trivial delay between human approval and authorisation.
Basket state is re-derived rather than frozen at approval time.
The mandate hash is not re-verified against the final basket at authorisation.

observable_signals.signal: Mandate hash does not bind to the basket actually authorised.
Settled amount has moved relative to the ceiling the human saw.
An unusually long or unusually short gap between mandate issuance and authorisation.
Content ingested after approval introduces a domain not present before it.

mitigations: Freeze the basket at approval and re-verify the hash binding at authorisation.
Cap the permitted interval between mandate issuance and use.
Treat any post-approval content ingestion as invalidating the approval.
references: Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - cart mandate binding
CWE-367 Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition

F1-08.name: Cross-mandate credential reuse
F1-08.actor: An operator with access to an agent runtime that holds more than one active mandate for the same customer.
F1-08.genai_enabler: Agents hold many concurrent authorisations - a grocery mandate, a travel mandate, a subscription mandate - and select among them at runtime. Selection is a planning decision, and planning decisions can be influenced.
F1-08.description: A payment token issued under one mandate is presented against a purchase belonging to another. Each mandate individually authorises spend, so no ceiling is breached and no signature is missing; what is wrong is the pairing. The attack converts a narrow, low-limit authorisation into whichever of the customer's mandates has the most headroom, without forging anything at all.
preconditions: Customer holds multiple concurrent mandates through one agent runtime.
Payment tokens are not cryptographically bound to the mandate that minted them.

observable_signals.signal: The presented token does not bind to the mandate cited in the authorisation.
One mandate hash is associated with transactions across unrelated categories and merchants.
The merchant is new to this customer despite the mandate being an established one.

mitigations: Bind every payment token to the mandate that issued it and verify at authorisation.
Scope tokens to a single mandate and a single settlement.
Alert on any mandate whose transactions span categories its scope never named.
references: Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - payment mandate binding
EMVCo Payment Tokenisation Specification - token domain restriction

F1-09.name: Human-present spoofing for liability shift
F1-09.actor: An operator of an agent or agent platform with an economic reason to claim human oversight it does not have — to skip step-up friction, to improve approval rates, or to move chargeback liability onto the issuer or the cardholder.
F1-09.genai_enabler: Presence has historically been evidenced by telemetry that was expensive to fake convincingly: cursor paths, dwell times, hesitation before commit. Generative models reproduce those distributions cheaply, so the assertion "a human was watching" degrades from evidence into an unverified claim.
F1-09.description: The authorisation asserts human_present, and supporting behavioural telemetry is synthesised to back the claim, so the transaction is treated as human-authorised: step-up is skipped, liability shifts, and the transaction inherits the lower scrutiny that supervised commerce earns. This vector is economically important out of proportion to its sophistication, because human_present is a liability flag as much as a risk flag — spoofing it does not merely evade a control, it relocates the loss. The tell is that forged telemetry is distributionally too clean: real humans hesitate irregularly, generators do not.
preconditions: Rail grants reduced authentication or shifted liability when human presence is asserted.
Presence is claimed by the agent rather than attested by an independent channel.
Behavioural telemetry is accepted without provenance or device attestation.

observable_signals.signal: human_present is asserted while no step-up authentication was performed or offered.
Consent signature is absent or unverified on a transaction claiming live human oversight.
Cursor entropy sits in an unnaturally narrow band relative to the human population — too regular to be a person.
Dwell time is implausibly short or suspiciously uniform for the basket size being approved.
Decision latency is below human reaction floors while presence is claimed.
The joint presence-telemetry vector falls outside the manifold of genuinely supervised sessions, even where each margin looks acceptable alone.

mitigations: Attest presence out-of-band (device-bound passkey, issuer app confirmation) rather than trusting an agent-asserted flag.
Bind liability shift to a verifiable authentication event, never to a self-declared boolean.
Rate-limit and monitor the human_present rate per agent and per platform; a platform at 100% presence is making a claim, not a measurement.
Retain presence telemetry for post-hoc distributional audit, so spoofing is detectable even after approval.
references: EMV 3-D Secure - authentication outcomes and liability shift conditions
Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - human-present and human-not-present transaction modes
Mastercard Agent Pay - agent identity and consent attestation (2025)

F1-10.name: Mandate replay and TTL abuse
F1-10.actor: Anyone who observes or retains a valid mandate artefact — a compromised sub-agent, a logging sidecar, a caching proxy, or an agent platform that keeps mandates longer than it should. No forgery capability is needed; the mandate is genuine, which is the point.
F1-10.genai_enabler: Agent architectures pass mandates between planners, tools and sub-agents as ordinary context, so a signed authorisation ends up in caches, transcripts and logs never designed to hold a bearer credential. Long-lived intent mandates make the reuse window wide enough to matter.
F1-10.description: A previously valid mandate is presented again — after its TTL has expired, more times than its scope allows, or by an agent other than the one it was issued to. Every signature verifies, because the artefact is authentic; the failure is one of freshness and single-use, not of cryptography. Replay is the classic bearer-token weakness reappearing in a new setting, and it is the cheapest F1 vector to run because it requires no injection, no social engineering, and no model access at all.
preconditions: Mandate artefacts are transportable and verify independently of the session that created them.
Mandate identifier or hash is not enforced as single-use at the network.
Issuance timestamp and TTL are carried but not authoritatively checked at authorisation.

observable_signals.signal: Authorisation arrives after the mandate's issuance time plus its TTL.
The same mandate hash appears on more authorisations than its scope permits.
Mandate age at authorisation is far outside the distribution for its mandate type.
Reuses arrive in a machine-regular cadence rather than the irregular spacing of genuine repeat purchases.
One mandate hash is presented by multiple distinct agent identifiers, or across unrelated customers.

mitigations: Enforce single-use or explicitly counted mandate identifiers at the network, with a replay cache covering the full TTL window.
Keep TTLs short and check them at authorisation against network time, not agent-supplied time.
Bind the mandate to the agent identity and session that requested it, so a leaked artefact is not portable.
Alert on mandate artefacts appearing in logs or caches; treat them as bearer credentials, because they are.
references: Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - mandate lifetime, identifiers and verification
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - excessive agency and insecure session handling

F1-11.name: Silent mandate renewal and TTL extension abuse
F1-11.actor: An operator who controls the agent or the platform component responsible for refreshing an expiring mandate.
F1-11.genai_enabler: Agents are built to be persistent and to avoid interrupting the human. An agent optimised not to nag will renew its own authority rather than ask, and will present that renewal as continuity of an existing arrangement.
F1-11.description: A short-lived mandate is meant to expire, forcing the human back into the loop. Instead it is renewed repeatedly without fresh consent, each renewal presented as a continuation. The mandate never technically expires, so the time-bound control that made a narrow scope safe silently becomes unbounded. This is a slow attack, and its signature lives in the cadence rather than in any single authorisation.
preconditions: Mandates can be extended or reissued without a fresh human consent event.
No cap on renewal count or on cumulative authorised lifetime.

observable_signals.signal: The same mandate lineage has been extended more times than policy allows.
Cumulative mandate age far exceeds the TTL the human originally agreed to.
Renewals arrive on a machine-regular cadence with no human-driven variance.
The mandate's behavioural profile drifts steadily away from where it started.

mitigations: Cap cumulative authorised lifetime, not just per-mandate TTL.
Require a fresh human consent event for renewal, never an agent-initiated one.
Report cumulative delegated authority back to the customer periodically.
references: Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - mandate lifetime and revocation
RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls - recurring mandates

F1-12.name: Multi-agent collusion under a single mandate
F1-12.actor: An operator running a coordinated set of agents that share one legitimately issued mandate between them.
F1-12.genai_enabler: Coordinating many agents against a shared constraint is a scheduling problem that generative planning solves cheaply. Each agent takes a slice of the budget and a schedule that keeps every individual authorisation unremarkable - a strategy that would previously have needed a human operator per account.
F1-12.description: One mandate, many executing agents. Each stays inside the per-transaction ceiling and each looks ordinary in isolation; together they consume authority far faster than the human intended, and they spread the footprint across agent identities so no single agent looks busy. The attack is invisible per-transaction and obvious in the graph, which is exactly the case the L4 layer exists to cover.
preconditions: A mandate that constrains per-transaction amount but not aggregate spend.
Multiple agent identities able to present the same mandate.

observable_signals.signal: One mandate hash is presented by several distinct agent identifiers.
An agent cluster shares a customer but no legitimate co-ownership relationship.
Aggregate authorisation rate for the customer spikes while each agent stays quiet.
The mandate's usage pattern is an outlier against the population of mandates of its type.

mitigations: Constrain aggregate spend per mandate, not only per transaction.
Bind a mandate to a single executing agent identity.
Score mandates at the mandate level rather than only at the transaction level.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM06 Excessive Agency
Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - mandate scope constraints

F2-13.name: GenAI synthetic identity onboarding
F2-13.actor: An organised fraud operation building portfolios of fabricated customers, each cultivated to look ordinary long enough to acquire credit, then monetised together in a coordinated bust-out.
F2-13.genai_enabler: The historic constraint on synthetic identity was per-identity cost: coherent documents, a plausible digital footprint, and a consistent life story took human effort. Generative models collapse that cost toward zero and, worse, remove the shared artefacts that used to link members of a batch — every identity can now be individually unique while the batch is still statistically and relationally correlated. The linkage moves from documents to behaviour.
F2-13.description: Fabricated customers pass onboarding, transact normally at low value to accumulate history and limit, then ramp sharply and disappear together. MANTIS models the transaction-stream consequences rather than the onboarding artefacts: the document-forensics problem is real but sits upstream of the authorisation message, so this card deliberately claims only what the schema can actually observe. What the stream does show is a cohort whose first transactions arrive suspiciously soon after account creation, whose devices and network paths overlap more than unrelated strangers' should, and whose spend ramps on a curve no organic customer follows.
preconditions: Onboarding accepts generated identity artefacts without independent source-of-truth verification.
Credit or transaction limits grow with observed tenure and repayment behaviour.
Multiple synthetic customers share some infrastructure - device, network path, or issuing BIN range.

observable_signals.signal: On the agentic variant, the agent acting for the identity carries no valid KYA registration.
Time from account creation to first transaction is far below the population norm for the segment.
Device or network fingerprint recurs across customers who have no other relationship.
Spend ramps monotonically toward the limit with none of the volatility of organic behaviour, then stops.
The identity sits in a graph component whose density and shared attributes are inconsistent with unrelated real customers.

mitigations: Verify identity against an authoritative source rather than against document plausibility, which generation now defeats.
Score cohorts, not individuals - synthetics are cheap alone and expensive as a correlated batch.
Hold limit growth behind behavioural evidence that is costly to fabricate over time, not behind tenure alone.
Re-verify at limit increases and at first high-value transaction, where the bust-out has to pass through.
references: US Federal Reserve - synthetic identity fraud definition and payments-industry guidance
FinCEN advisories on identity-related exploitation of financial institutions
RBI / NPCI onboarding and KYC circulars (India market context)

F2-14.name: Unregistered and forged Know-Your-Agent credentials
F2-14.actor: An operator standing up agent identities that the network has never registered, or presenting a credential that does not resolve to a real registry entry.
F2-14.genai_enabler: Agent identity is new, thinly enforced, and inconsistently checked during rollout. Generative tooling makes it trivial to produce large numbers of plausible agent identities, platform strings and credential-shaped tokens, so the cost of testing which acquirers actually verify falls to near zero.
F2-14.description: The Know-Your-Agent registry is the agentic rail's equivalent of merchant onboarding: it is what makes an agent identity mean anything. This attack transacts with an agent that is simply not in it, or with a credential that is well-formed but unresolvable, and relies on acceptance paths that treat KYA as advisory. The difficulty is that a real rollout has a legitimate tail of unregistered agents, so the naive rule "unregistered equals fraud" is both wrong and expensive. What separates the two is everything else about the session, not the flag on its own.
preconditions: Acceptance path treats an absent or unresolvable KYA credential as non-blocking.
No positive verification of the credential against the registry at authorisation.

observable_signals.signal: Agent presents no KYA credential, or one that does not resolve to a registry entry.
Agent platform string is one never seen before across the whole portfolio.
Agent identifier has no transaction history and no established customer relationship.
The session sits far from the legitimate agentic population on every behavioural axis at once.
The unregistered agent identity is one of many sharing a device or address neighbourhood.

mitigations: Verify the KYA credential against the registry at authorisation, not at onboarding only.
Apply a lower authority ceiling to unregistered agents rather than a blanket decline.
Score the credential alongside behavioural evidence, never as a standalone rule.
references: Mastercard Agent Pay - agent registration and Know-Your-Agent
Google AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) - agent identity attestation

F2-15.name: Deepfake liveness bypass at video KYC
F2-15.actor: An operator onboarding an account under a synthetic or stolen identity through a remote video verification step.
F2-15.genai_enabler: Real-time face and voice synthesis has moved from research demo to commodity, and remote onboarding was designed on the assumption that a live video feed is evidence of a live person. That assumption no longer holds, and the cost of breaking it has collapsed.
F2-15.description: Remote onboarding is the front door to a payment credential. This attack defeats the liveness check itself, so the account that emerges is fully verified by the issuer's own records and carries no onboarding-time signal at all. Nothing about the resulting transactions looks unusual in isolation; what gives the account away is the behavioural profile of the portfolio it belongs to and the funding pattern that follows onboarding.
preconditions: Remote video or selfie-based identity verification with no independent document or bureau check.
Liveness detection that has not been hardened against synthetic media.

observable_signals.signal: A cohort of accounts onboarded in a narrow window shares device and network characteristics.
Early transaction behaviour is unusually uniform for a supposedly independent account.
Account tenure is short relative to the authority and limits it is exercising.
The account's overall behavioural profile is an outlier against genuinely new customers.

mitigations: Pair liveness with an independent bureau or document channel that synthetic media cannot reach.
Hold newly onboarded accounts at reduced limits until behaviour accumulates.
Monitor onboarding cohorts as a graph, not as independent applications.
references: RBI Master Direction - Know Your Customer, video-based customer identification
NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology

F2-16.name: Agent-farm account bootstrapping for bust-out
F2-16.actor: An operator running a portfolio of synthetic accounts, each paired with its own agent identity, cultivated for a coordinated bust-out.
F2-16.genai_enabler: Bust-out fraud has always been limited by the human labour of maintaining plausible accounts through a cultivation period. Agents remove that limit: a portfolio of hundreds can be cultivated concurrently, each with individually plausible behaviour, at a cost that no longer scales with headcount.
F2-16.description: Accounts are opened, behave impeccably for a cultivation period, accrue limit increases, and then draw down together. The bust-out itself is easy to see and far too late to matter. The detectable phase is the cultivation phase, where the tell is not any individual account's behaviour - which is by construction unremarkable - but the unnatural *similarity* between accounts that should have nothing to do with each other.
preconditions: Automated or lightly reviewed account opening at volume.
Limit increases driven by behavioural history without portfolio-level review.

observable_signals.signal: Accounts that share no stated relationship show near-identical spending rhythms.
A dense component of customers, devices and merchants with no organic bridging structure.
Agent identities cluster onto a small number of platforms and address ranges.
Cultivation-phase behaviour is too well-behaved relative to the genuine population.

mitigations: Review limit increases at portfolio level, not per account.
Cluster new accounts on device, address and agent-platform evidence before granting authority.
Treat abnormally low variance in behaviour as a risk signal rather than a good one.
references: FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators
RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls

F2-17.name: Generated-document merchant onboarding
F2-17.actor: An operator onboarding a merchant account on fabricated incorporation, address and banking evidence, in order to become the acceptance side of the fraud rather than the issuing side.
F2-17.genai_enabler: Document generation at scale, in the correct regional formats, with internally consistent details across a whole application pack, is now a commodity capability. Merchant onboarding review was calibrated against a world where producing a convincing pack took real effort.
F2-17.description: Controlling a merchant of record is the most valuable position in a payment fraud, because it makes the attacker the party that receives the funds. This card covers acquiring that position through fabricated onboarding evidence. The merchant then operates normally for a period before being used to accept attacker-directed volume - which is what links it to the F6 laundering family.
preconditions: Merchant onboarding relies primarily on submitted documentary evidence.
Limited post-onboarding monitoring of merchant behaviour against its declared category.

observable_signals.signal: Merchant is newly onboarded relative to the volume and ticket size it is processing.
Actual transaction mix does not match the category the merchant registered under.
Merchant sits in a cluster of entities sharing registration and settlement characteristics.
Customer base is unusually narrow and unusually loyal for a new merchant.

mitigations: Verify incorporation and banking evidence against authoritative registries, not the submitted pack.
Hold new merchants at reduced settlement limits pending behavioural history.
Monitor realised transaction mix against the declared category continuously.
references: FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators
Mastercard Rules - merchant onboarding and monitoring obligations

F2-18.name: Synthetic-agent reputation farming
F2-18.actor: An operator building agent identities whose registry standing and transaction history are cultivated specifically to be spent later.
F2-18.genai_enabler: Any reputation system that rewards history creates an incentive to manufacture history. Agents can transact continuously, cheaply and plausibly, so an agent reputation can be farmed on a timescale and at a cost that a human-operated account never could.
F2-18.description: This is F2-16 aimed at the agent layer rather than the account layer. An agent identity accumulates a clean record of small, real, unremarkable transactions until its standing earns it higher limits and lighter scrutiny, and only then is that standing spent. The attack is an argument against treating agent reputation as a monotonically accumulating asset, and the detectable phase is again the farming phase rather than the payoff.
preconditions: Agent standing or limits are earned through transaction history.
Reputation accrues without reference to who ultimately controls the agent.

observable_signals.signal: Transaction history is unusually regular and unusually low-variance for its volume.
Ticket sizes cluster tightly just under the thresholds that trigger review.
Agent behaviour shifts abruptly once standing has been achieved.
Farmed agents share settlement counterparties with each other but not with the wider population.

mitigations: Decay agent standing over time rather than accumulating it indefinitely.
Weight reputation by counterparty diversity, not by transaction count.
Re-verify control of an agent identity before granting materially higher authority.
references: Mastercard Agent Pay - agent registration and Know-Your-Agent
MITRE ATLAS - adversarial threat landscape for AI systems

F3-19.name: Digital-arrest scam
F3-19.actor: An organised social-engineering crew impersonating law enforcement or regulators, operating at call-centre scale against a victim list, with mule accounts prepared to receive and disperse.
F3-19.genai_enabler: Voice cloning and real-time translation remove the two things that used to break the illusion: an accent that did not match the claimed agency, and a script that could not adapt when the victim pushed back. A model can sustain a coercive, procedurally plausible interrogation for hours, in the victim's own language, and can be run against many victims at once.
F3-19.description: The victim is convinced they are under investigation and held in a prolonged session — often on video, told not to hang up or contact anyone — until they transfer funds to accounts described as "verification" custody. Critically the victim authorises every payment themselves, so authentication succeeds, the device is the usual device, and the credential is genuine. Nothing in the authentication layer will ever flag this; only behaviour and beneficiary structure will. Where the victim's own agent is drawn into the pretext, the coercive content lands in the provenance chain and becomes directly readable by L3 — on classic rails no such text exists, and the card claims no L3 signal there.
preconditions: Victim retains full control of their credentials and authenticates normally.
Receiving accounts are reachable in near-real-time and can be emptied quickly.
No cooling-off or out-of-band confirmation applies to first-time high-value beneficiaries.

observable_signals.signal: Transfer amount sits far above the customer's own historic ceiling, not merely above a population threshold.
Beneficiary has no prior relationship with the customer and receives an unusually large first payment.
Several transfers arrive in a tight burst, frequently escalating, within a single sustained session.
On the agent-mediated variant, ingested content carries authority-impersonation and urgency framing.
The receiving account collects from many unrelated victims and disperses immediately - the mule signature.

mitigations: Impose a cooling-off window and out-of-band confirmation on first high-value payments to a new beneficiary.
Interdict in-session with a scam warning tuned to this pattern; the victim is authenticated, so the intervention has to reach the human, not the credential.
Score beneficiary-side fan-in and dispersal velocity, which the crew cannot hide the way it hides the victim-side signal.
Share mule-account intelligence across institutions, since the receiving side is the only part of the operation that is reused.
references: RBI and Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre public advisories on 'digital arrest' fraud
NPCI UPI risk and beneficiary-cooling-off guidance
FATF typologies - money mule networks and layering

F3-20.name: Voice-clone authorised push payment fraud
F3-20.actor: An operator who contacts the victim impersonating a family member, a bank official or an employer, using a cloned voice, and instructs them to send money themselves.
F3-20.genai_enabler: Voice cloning from a few seconds of public audio removes the single most reliable trust cue in remote social engineering. The victim is not tricked into revealing a credential; they are convinced by a voice they recognise, and they authorise the payment themselves.
F3-20.description: Authorised push payment fraud is uniquely hard for a payment network because the customer is genuinely the one paying. Authentication passes because it should - the customer really is the customer, and the device really is theirs. Everything that identifies the transaction as fraud is contextual: an unprecedented counterparty, an amount out of line with the customer's history, a payment made at an hour and a pace that does not match how this person normally behaves. This is the clearest case in the atlas for why behavioural and graph features matter more than credential checks.
preconditions: A payment rail on which the customer can push funds to a new counterparty in one session.
No cooling-off period or counterparty confirmation for first-time payees.

observable_signals.signal: Payment to a counterparty the customer has never transacted with before.
Amount is a severe outlier against this customer's own distribution, not just the population's.
Transaction sits far outside the customer's normal hour-of-day pattern.
Rapid sequence of escalating payments to the same new counterparty.
Beneficiary receives from many unrelated customers who have no other connection to each other.
The session's behavioural profile departs from the customer's established baseline.

mitigations: Impose a cooling-off period and confirmation step for first-time high-value payees.
Score beneficiary accounts on inbound fan-in from unrelated senders.
Surface a plain-language warning at the moment of payment, not in a policy document.
references: UK Payment Systems Regulator - APP fraud performance report
Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) - advisories on impersonation fraud

F3-21.name: Task and investment scam payout orchestration
F3-21.actor: An operator running a task-based or investment scam in which the victim is induced to make escalating payments against promised returns.
F3-21.genai_enabler: Sustaining a convincing, personalised, multi-week conversation with hundreds of victims simultaneously was the binding constraint on this fraud. Generative conversation removes it, and also personalises the escalation schedule to each victim's demonstrated willingness to pay.
F3-21.description: The victim makes a series of payments, each individually justified by the scam's internal logic and each one larger than the last. Early payments may even receive small real returns, which is what makes the later ones possible. From the network's side the signature is the escalation curve and the concentration of many unrelated victims onto a small set of beneficiaries.
preconditions: Victim retains control of their own account and authorises each payment.
Beneficiary accounts can receive from many unrelated senders without review.

observable_signals.signal: A monotonically escalating payment sequence to the same beneficiary.
Beneficiary shows high inbound fan-in from senders with no relationship to each other.
Customer's payment behaviour departs sharply from their own long-run baseline.
Beneficiary sits in a component that receives broadly and pays out narrowly.

mitigations: Score beneficiary accounts on inbound fan-in and onward concentration.
Intervene on escalation patterns rather than on single-payment thresholds.
Share beneficiary risk signals across institutions where the framework permits.
references: FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators
Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) - advisories on investment fraud

F3-22.name: Conversational romance-scam escalation
F3-22.actor: An operator running long-horizon relationship-based social engineering, maintaining many concurrent victims through generated conversation.
F3-22.genai_enabler: The economics of romance fraud were previously bounded by how many relationships one operator could sustain. Generative conversation lifts that bound entirely while improving consistency of persona, and makes the approach viable in more languages and dialects than an operator could personally speak.
F3-22.description: A relationship is cultivated over weeks or months and then monetised through requests framed as emergencies. The payments themselves are ordinary person-to-person transfers made willingly by the victim. What is detectable is the shape of the relationship in the transaction graph - a first-time counterparty who rapidly becomes the customer's dominant payee - and the departure of the customer's behaviour from their own history.
preconditions: Person-to-person rails available for transfers to a newly added counterparty.
No aggregate view of a customer's exposure to a single new beneficiary.

observable_signals.signal: A newly added counterparty rapidly becomes the customer's largest payee by value.
Transfers to a counterparty with whom the customer shares no device, address or history.
Beneficiary account receives from multiple unrelated victims in parallel.
Customer's transaction profile drifts persistently away from their established baseline.

mitigations: Track cumulative exposure to each beneficiary and warn on rapid concentration.
Apply extended confirmation to newly added high-value payees.
Score beneficiaries on parallel inbound relationships with unrelated senders.
references: UK Payment Systems Regulator - APP fraud performance report
FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators

F3-23.name: Fake storefront seeded into agent search
F3-23.actor: An operator who stands up a merchant presence designed to be selected by shopping agents rather than browsed by humans.
F3-23.genai_enabler: Agents select merchants by reading structured product data and machine-facing content, and they do so without the human cues - visual polish, brand familiarity, review plausibility - that a person applies unconsciously. A storefront optimised for machine selection can be generated at negligible cost and needs to convince nothing but a retrieval step.
F3-23.description: The storefront exists to be chosen by an agent operating under a legitimate mandate. The customer authorised the purchase, the agent stayed within scope, and the goods never arrive. This is a merchant-side attack that arrives through the agentic rail, and it is why merchant reputation has to be assessed by the network rather than inferred by the agent that is being targeted.
preconditions: Agent merchant selection driven by machine-readable content without independent reputation checks.
Merchant onboarding that permits rapid establishment of a new acceptance presence.

observable_signals.signal: Merchant is very new relative to the volume it is suddenly receiving.
Merchant domain appears in provenance chains with no prior history anywhere in the portfolio.
Merchant is reached almost exclusively through agent traffic, never through human sessions.
Merchant appears abruptly across many unrelated customers at once.

mitigations: Require network-side merchant reputation before an agent may settle with a new merchant.
Hold first-time agent-selected merchants at reduced limits.
Feed merchant age and traffic composition into the agent's selection constraints.
references: Mastercard Rules - merchant onboarding and monitoring obligations
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM01 Prompt Injection

F3-24.name: Invoice redirection against an agent procurement flow
F3-24.actor: An operator who compromises or impersonates a supplier relationship and substitutes their own settlement details into a procurement flow an agent executes.
F3-24.genai_enabler: Business email compromise depended on convincing correspondence in the right register with the right history. Generation makes that cheap and consistent, and an agent executing procurement will act on a well-formed instruction without the vague unease a human accounts-payable clerk might feel.
F3-24.description: The purchase is real, the supplier relationship is real, and the amount is expected. Only the beneficiary has changed. Because the agent is executing an approved workflow, every control that checks whether the payment was authorised passes. The detectable change is that a long-standing counterparty relationship has silently acquired a new settlement destination.
preconditions: Supplier settlement details can be updated inside the flow the agent executes.
No out-of-band verification of a change to banking details.

observable_signals.signal: A long-standing supplier relationship settles to a destination never used before.
Payment amount matches history while the counterparty identity does not.
Instruction content carries urgency and confidentiality framing atypical of the relationship.
New beneficiary sits in a component associated with other recently changed relationships.

mitigations: Verify any change of settlement details out of band, on a previously known channel.
Freeze newly changed beneficiaries for a fixed window before first settlement.
Deny agents the authority to update supplier banking details at all.
references: FBI IC3 - Business Email Compromise public service announcements
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM06 Excessive Agency

F3-25.name: Deepfake executive authorisation of a corporate mandate
F3-25.actor: An operator impersonating a senior executive over synthetic video or voice in order to have a high-authority mandate issued.
F3-25.genai_enabler: Real-time synthetic video has made the live call - historically the escalation channel used to *verify* a suspicious instruction - into an attack surface. The control that was supposed to catch impersonation is now the vector.
F3-25.description: Rather than attacking a payment, this attacks the issuance of authority. A mandate with a wide scope and a high ceiling is granted because a convincing executive asked for it on a call. Everything downstream is then legitimate: the mandate is properly signed, properly scoped, and properly used. Detection has to happen at issuance, or in the anomalous shape of the mandate itself relative to the organisation's normal delegation patterns.
preconditions: Mandates of material scope can be issued on the strength of a synchronous call.
No multi-party approval for high-authority delegation.

observable_signals.signal: Mandate scope and ceiling are extreme outliers against the organisation's normal issuance.
Mandate issued outside normal business hours or approval channels.
Mandate is used almost immediately after issuance and then not again.
Beneficiary of the resulting spend has no prior relationship with the organisation.

mitigations: Require multi-party approval for mandates above an authority threshold, never a single call.
Bind mandate issuance to an authenticated channel rather than to a synchronous conversation.
Alert on mandates whose scope is an outlier against the organisation's own history.
references: FBI IC3 - Business Email Compromise public service announcements
NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology

F3-26.name: Support-impersonation mandate handover
F3-26.actor: An operator impersonating customer support or an agent-platform vendor, persuading the victim to grant a mandate to an agent the attacker controls.
F3-26.genai_enabler: "Let my assistant sort that out for you" is a natural, helpful-sounding request in an agentic world, and a generated support persona can sustain the interaction convincingly. The attack asks the victim for delegated authority rather than for a credential, which is a request that does not trip the instincts people have been trained to have about passwords and OTPs.
F3-26.description: The victim is talked into issuing a genuine mandate to an attacker-controlled agent, usually framed as necessary to resolve a problem. Because the mandate is genuine, every cryptographic control passes. What is anomalous is the recipient: an agent with no history with this customer, on a platform they have never used, receiving authority within moments of a support interaction. Public awareness of credential phishing does not transfer to this, which is what makes it worth naming separately.
preconditions: Customer can issue a mandate to an arbitrary agent identity without a cooling-off period.
No prominent disclosure of what authority a mandate actually confers.

observable_signals.signal: Mandate granted to an agent with no prior relationship to this customer.
Receiving agent runs on a platform the customer has never used.
Mandate is exercised almost immediately after issuance.
The recipient agent identity is receiving mandates from many unrelated customers at once.

mitigations: Impose a cooling-off period before a newly granted mandate can be exercised.
Show the customer, in plain language, what authority they are about to delegate.
Rate-limit and review agent identities accumulating mandates from unrelated customers.
references: Mastercard Agent Pay - agent registration and Know-Your-Agent
Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) - advisories on impersonation fraud

F4-27.name: Adaptive BIN attack
F4-27.actor: A technically capable fraud operation with a corpus of card credentials and enough merchant access to observe authorisation outcomes. The distinguishing capability is not credential supply but the feedback loop: they can see which attempts approve.
F4-27.genai_enabler: Approve and decline responses are a free oracle. An LLM-driven search loop turns that oracle into a hill-climb over the defender's decision surface, proposing amount bands, MCCs, merchant types and timing that keep scores under threshold. What used to be a fraudster's slow intuition becomes an automated parameter search running continuously against production.
F4-27.description: Rather than maximising value per attempt, the attacker probes: small authorisations spread across a BIN range, varying amount, merchant category and hour, reading the decline pattern to infer where the boundary sits, then concentrating value in the region that approves. The resulting fraud looks ordinary one transaction at a time — that is the objective function — and is only visible in aggregate structure across the BIN. This card is the reference vector for the adversarial loop in Pillar 3: it is the family the evolutionary adversary attacks first, and the one whose evasion rate we report across generations.
preconditions: Attacker holds many credentials sharing BIN ranges.
Authorisation outcomes are observable to the attacker at low cost and low latency.
Detection thresholds are static between retrains, giving the search a stationary target.

observable_signals.signal: Attempt rate within a BIN range spikes far above its baseline, spread thinly across many card numbers.
Amounts cluster in narrow probe bands rather than following the merchant's natural ticket distribution.
Decline ratio for the BIN rises sharply during the search phase, then falls as the attacker converges.
Approved traffic drifts toward a low-density region of feature space - the gap the search found - which supervised layers score as benign because nothing there was ever labelled.
One BIN range fans out across an implausible set of unrelated merchants in a short window.

mitigations: Rate-limit and score at BIN-range level, not only per card, so thin-spread probing still accumulates evidence.
Randomise or hysteresis-damp thresholds so the oracle returns a noisy gradient instead of a clean one.
Retrain on a cadence shorter than the attacker's search time, which is the entire premise of the MANTIS closed loop.
Weight the unsupervised novelty layer explicitly at fusion, since a successful search is by construction invisible to the supervised layer.
references: Card scheme BIN attack / enumeration monitoring guidance
Adversarial machine learning: evasion attacks under black-box query access (literature background)
NIST AI 100-2 - Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy (evasion, model querying)

F4-28.name: Threshold probing and just-under structuring
F4-28.actor: An operator who can observe approve and decline outcomes, and use them to locate the amount thresholds a risk engine is using.
F4-28.genai_enabler: Threshold discovery is a search problem, and search is what an agent is for. An automated adversary can binary-search the decline boundary across amounts, categories and rails in hours, then hold every subsequent transaction just underneath it. That work previously required a patient human operator and a lot of burned cards.
F4-28.description: Risk engines use amount thresholds, and thresholds are discoverable by anyone who can observe outcomes. Once located, the attacker splits value into transactions that sit deliberately just below each boundary, extracting the same total while never crossing a line that triggers review. The tell is not any individual amount, since each is unremarkable by construction, but the unnatural density of amounts hugging a boundary that means nothing at all to a genuine customer.
preconditions: Decline outcomes are observable to the party submitting the transaction.
Risk policy uses fixed amount thresholds rather than smooth, randomised or contextual ones.

observable_signals.signal: Amounts cluster just below a policy threshold far more tightly than the population warrants.
A value that would once have been one transaction now arrives as several within a short window.
Split transactions share a merchant and category that the customer history does not support.
The amount distribution for this entity fits the population log-normal shape poorly.
Probing leaves a trail of near-boundary attempts spread across several BINs or agents.

mitigations: Randomise or smooth thresholds so a boundary cannot be located by observation.
Score aggregate value over a window rather than per-transaction amount.
Rate-limit and alert on repeated near-boundary attempts from one entity.
references: FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators (structuring)
NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology

F4-29.name: Attribution-guided feature-space evasion
F4-29.actor: An operator with access to detector explanations, through a scoring API that returns reasons, a leaked model, or inference from decline patterns, who uses them to reshape attacks toward the features carrying least weight.
F4-29.genai_enabler: Attribution methods were built to make models auditable, and they work just as well for an attacker. Combined with generative mutation they turn evasion into a guided search: read which features drove the score, perturb those, preserve the payload effect, resubmit. Each generation is cheaper and better targeted than the last.
F4-29.description: This is the card the closed loop is built around, and the one that makes MANTIS a lab rather than a demo. The adversary reads the detector attribution output, identifies which features are carrying the decision, and mutates along the directions of least resistance while preserving the economic effect of the attack. The detector retrains on what it caught, the adversary adapts again, and the evasion rate across generations is the curve worth showing. The defensive point is that a single static model loses this game, and what holds is layer diversity: a mutation that defeats a gradient-boosted boundary rarely also satisfies a deterministic mandate rule.
preconditions: Attacker can observe scores, reasons or declines with enough fidelity to guide a search.
Detection rests on a few high-weight features that can be perturbed independently.

observable_signals.signal: Feature values drift toward the decision boundary across generations while the outcome holds.
Attack instances cluster in a region of feature space that is sparse in legitimate traffic.
Events sit far from the training manifold despite scoring low on the supervised model.
Perturbation reshapes the tabular features but leaves the mandate arithmetic violated.
Provenance and text evidence survive perturbation aimed at the tabular layer.

mitigations: Do not expose per-feature reasons on an unauthenticated or high-rate scoring path.
Keep deterministic mandate rules in the fusion so tabular evasion alone is never sufficient.
Retrain against adversary output and report the evasion rate across generations.
Prefer layer diversity to single-model accuracy; the layers fail in different directions.
references: NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology
MITRE ATLAS - adversarial threat landscape for AI systems

F4-30.name: Velocity shaping against count-window rules
F4-30.actor: An operator who has inferred the count-and-window shape of a velocity rule and schedules activity to stay underneath it.
F4-30.genai_enabler: Scheduling many actions against a known constraint, across many accounts and many windows at once, is exactly the combinatorial planning that is now cheap. The attacker does not need the rule exactly; a few hundred probes reveal enough of its shape to schedule around.
F4-30.description: Where F4-28 shapes amounts against value thresholds, this shapes timing against count thresholds. Transactions are spaced so no rolling window ever holds enough of them to trip a rule, and are spread across cards, devices or agents so no single entity accumulates a count. The residue is a cadence that is too even: real customers cluster and then go quiet, and an attacker metering themselves against a window does neither.
preconditions: Velocity rules use fixed counts over fixed windows.
Counting is scoped per entity in a way that spreading across entities defeats.

observable_signals.signal: Inter-arrival gaps are far more regular than a genuine customer ever produces.
Activity resumes immediately after each rolling window expires.
Counts sit just below the rule limit across many consecutive windows.
Related entities share a footprint while each individually stays under the limit.

mitigations: Use overlapping and randomised windows rather than fixed non-overlapping ones.
Count at the entity-cluster level, not only at the card or agent level.
Treat abnormally regular cadence as a signal in its own right.
references: NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology
FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators

F4-31.name: Feedback-loop label poisoning
F4-31.actor: An operator who can influence the labels a detector learns from, typically by generating disputes or confirmations that flow back into training data.
F4-31.genai_enabler: Producing large volumes of plausible, individually reasonable dispute narratives is now cheap, and fraud models retrain on outcome labels derived from exactly those disputes. The attack targets the training pipeline rather than the model.
F4-31.description: If a detector learns from dispute outcomes, then whoever can shape dispute outcomes can shape the detector. Systematically mislabelling a region of feature space teaches the model that the region is benign, opening a corridor for later attacks. This is slow, indirect, and among the hardest attacks to attribute, because by the time it works the evidence lives in the model weights rather than in the transaction stream.
preconditions: Model retrains on labels derived from customer disputes or downstream outcomes.
No provenance weighting or review of label sources before they enter training.

observable_signals.signal: Dispute rate for a narrow feature region diverges sharply from its neighbours.
Disputing accounts cluster on shared devices, addresses or agent platforms.
Model performance decays in a localised region between retrains rather than uniformly.
Dispute narratives are unusually uniform in structure across unrelated customers.

mitigations: Weight training labels by the provenance and independence of their source.
Hold out a curated, manually adjudicated evaluation set that feedback cannot reach.
Monitor per-region performance between retrains, not only aggregate metrics.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning
NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology

F4-32.name: Decision-boundary mapping through probe transactions
F4-32.actor: An operator submitting low-value transactions purely to learn the shape of the decision surface, with no interest in the goods.
F4-32.genai_enabler: Model extraction is a query-efficiency problem, and an agent can issue and interpret structured probes far faster than a human. What used to be a slow, expensive reconnaissance phase becomes a short automated one whose output is a usable local model of the defender.
F4-32.description: Before the attack proper, the attacker maps the defence. Small, cheap transactions are varied systematically across amount, category, rail, timing and mandate shape, and the responses are used to reconstruct the boundary. The reconnaissance is nearly free and, taken one transaction at a time, entirely unremarkable. It is visible only as a pattern of systematic variation that no real customer would ever produce.
preconditions: Attacker can submit transactions and observe outcomes at low cost.
Decline responses differentiate enough to be informative.

observable_signals.signal: Systematic variation across one feature at a time while the others are held fixed.
Repeated low-value attempts across many BINs with an unusual amount spread.
High decline rate concentrated on one entity over a short window.
Probe traffic occupies a region of feature space that legitimate traffic does not.

mitigations: Return uniform decline responses that do not differentiate the reason.
Rate-limit and alert on entities generating systematic variation patterns.
Add calibrated randomness to borderline decisions so a boundary cannot be traced.
references: MITRE ATLAS - adversarial threat landscape for AI systems
NIST AI 100-2 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology

F5-33.name: Tool-descriptor poisoning
F5-33.actor: An operator who controls the metadata of a tool an agent may call, or who can publish a tool into a registry the agent discovers from.
F5-33.genai_enabler: An agent decides which tool to call by reading its description, and that description is untrusted text arriving from outside the trust boundary. The descriptor is not data the agent processes, it is guidance the agent acts on, which makes tool metadata a first-class injection surface that has no equivalent in conventional software.
F5-33.description: A tool description is written to steer the agent toward a particular payment behaviour: preferring one settlement path, treating a substitution as equivalent, or skipping a confirmation the human expects. The agent is functioning exactly as designed, and the mandate is intact; the corruption is in what the agent was told the tools mean. The payload is short and its effect is visible in the deliberation trace and the tool-call sequence, which is where the detection lives.
preconditions: Agent selects tools using descriptions it does not independently verify.
Tool metadata can be modified or published without review.

observable_signals.signal: Tool metadata carries imperative, agent-directed language rather than neutral description.
Tool-call count departs sharply from the norm for this task and merchant.
Deliberation collapses relative to comparable purchases of the same size.
Settled merchant or category falls outside the mandate the human agreed to.
The provenance chain includes a registry or descriptor source new to this customer.

mitigations: Pin tool descriptors by digest and re-verify before use; treat a change as a new tool.
Strip or quarantine instruction-shaped text in tool metadata before the planner sees it.
Enforce payment constraints outside the agent, so a poisoned descriptor cannot widen scope.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM01 Prompt Injection
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM05 Supply Chain Vulnerabilities

F5-34.name: Agent-platform compromise and mass mandate minting
F5-34.actor: An operator who has compromised an agent platform and can act with the authority the platform holds over its whole customer base.
F5-34.genai_enabler: Agent platforms concentrate delegated payment authority for many customers behind one operational boundary. That concentration is new. Compromising one platform now yields spending authority across its entire user base, which is a blast radius no single merchant breach has ever offered.
F5-34.description: This is the supply-chain case for the agentic rail, and the one with the worst ratio of effort to yield. Every mandate the platform mints is technically valid, correctly signed, and correctly scoped; the compromise is upstream of every cryptographic control. Nothing about an individual authorisation is wrong. What is wrong is the population: one platform issuing far more authority, far faster, across far more unrelated customers than it ever has before. Only a portfolio-level view sees it, which is the argument for scoring at the platform level and not only at the transaction level.
preconditions: A platform can mint or exercise mandates on behalf of many customers.
No per-platform rate limiting or anomaly detection on mandate issuance.

observable_signals.signal: Mandate issuance rate for one platform is a severe outlier against its own history.
Many unrelated customers transact through one platform in a tight window.
Newly minted mandates are exercised almost immediately after issuance.
Affected customers share nothing except the platform, forming a star in the entity graph.
The platform behavioural profile shifts abruptly away from its established baseline.

mitigations: Rate-limit mandate issuance per platform and alert on deviation from its own baseline.
Require customer-side confirmation for mandates above an authority threshold.
Give issuers a platform-level kill switch that does not require blocking each customer.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM05 Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Mastercard Agent Pay - agent registration and Know-Your-Agent

F5-35.name: Model supply-chain substitution
F5-35.actor: An operator who can substitute the planning model an agent runs on, whether by swapping weights, redirecting an inference endpoint, or publishing a compromised model artefact into a shared registry.
F5-35.genai_enabler: The planner is the decision-maker, and it arrives as an opaque artefact from a supply chain that is far less mature than the one for conventional software. A substituted planner makes different decisions while every surrounding system reports normal.
F5-35.description: Rather than manipulating the agent inputs, this replaces its judgement. A substituted planner can be made to prefer particular merchants, to accept substitutions it should refuse, or to under-weight its own guardrails, all while every log, credential and mandate looks correct. Detection has to be behavioural and population-level, because there is nothing wrong with any individual authorisation to find.
preconditions: Model artefacts or inference endpoints can be changed without attestation.
No behavioural regression testing of the planner against a known baseline.

observable_signals.signal: Merchant selection distribution shifts across a platform without a corresponding demand change.
Deliberation latency distribution shifts for the platform as a whole.
The platform behavioural profile departs from its established baseline population.
A small merchant set gains share simultaneously across unrelated customers.

mitigations: Attest model artefacts by digest and verify at load, refusing unpinned sources.
Run behavioural regression tests on the planner before promotion.
Monitor platform-level merchant selection distributions for unexplained drift.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM05 Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
MITRE ATLAS - adversarial threat landscape for AI systems

F5-36.name: Persistent memory and context-store poisoning
F5-36.actor: An operator who can write into an agent long-term memory or retrieval store, usually via content the agent has previously ingested and chosen to retain.
F5-36.genai_enabler: Agents are given persistent memory so they can be useful across sessions. That same persistence means a single successful injection need not be repeated: it is stored, retrieved and re-applied indefinitely, and it survives the session in which it arrived.
F5-36.description: Where F1-01 injects at read time and affects one transaction, this implants an instruction that persists. The provenance chain of the *later* transaction may look entirely clean, because the poisoned content was ingested days earlier and now arrives through the retrieval path instead. That decoupling of ingestion from effect is what makes it hard: the causal evidence is no longer adjacent to the transaction that shows the symptom.
preconditions: Agent maintains persistent memory or a retrieval store across sessions.
Stored content is not re-sanitised at retrieval time.

observable_signals.signal: Retrieved memory content carries instruction-shaped rather than factual text.
Scope excursions recur for one customer with no fresh injection in the chain.
The transaction provenance chain is unusually short given the decision complexity.
Behavioural drift persists across sessions rather than resolving between them.

mitigations: Sanitise content at retrieval time, not only at ingestion time.
Keep provenance on stored memories so a later effect can be traced to its origin.
Expire and re-verify long-lived memories that influence payment decisions.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM01 Prompt Injection
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses

F5-37.name: Rogue payment connector in the tool chain
F5-37.actor: An operator who can install or advertise a payment-capable connector into an agent tool chain, either as a new component or as a wrapper around a legitimate one.
F5-37.genai_enabler: Agents are designed to extend themselves with new capabilities at runtime, and the barrier to publishing a connector is far lower than the barrier to becoming a payment service provider. A capability that can move money now enters the chain through a channel built for convenience rather than for settlement assurance.
F5-37.description: Where F5-33 poisons what a tool claims to do, this introduces an unauthorised tool that actually moves money, or interposes one in front of a legitimate connector. The mandate may be entirely valid; the settlement path is not. Because the connector sits inside the agent runtime, the fraud is visible to the network only through the destination and the shape of the settlement, not through anything about the authorisation itself.
preconditions: Agent runtime permits addition of payment-capable tools without review.
No allow-list binding payment execution to approved connectors.

observable_signals.signal: Settlement is routed through a path never previously used by this platform.
Tool-call sequence includes a payment-capable component absent from the approved set.
Beneficiary concentration rises across otherwise unrelated customers of one platform.
Authorisation is well-formed while the settlement destination is anomalous for the merchant.

mitigations: Allow-list payment-capable connectors and refuse execution through any other.
Bind settlement destination to the merchant of record and verify at authorisation.
Require attestation of every tool that can initiate a payment.
references: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications - LLM05 Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Mastercard Rules - payment facilitator and settlement obligations

F6-38.name: Agentic mule-network fan-out
F6-38.actor: An operator coordinating a network of mule accounts through which proceeds are dispersed and recombined.
F6-38.genai_enabler: Layering has always been limited by the coordination cost of running many accounts on a schedule. Agents remove that cost: hundreds of accounts can be operated concurrently, each with individually plausible timing and amounts, and the routing can be re-planned continuously as accounts are frozen.
F6-38.description: Funds enter a small number of collection accounts, fan out across many mules, and recombine downstream. Every hop is a small, ordinary transfer that would never be flagged alone. The structure is only visible as a structure: a characteristic fan-out then fan-in topology with short dwell time at each hop, and a set of accounts whose only connection to each other is the money moving between them. This is the clearest case in the atlas for the graph layer, and the reason L4 is on the list at all.
preconditions: Person-to-person rails permitting rapid onward transfer.
Account-level monitoring with no network-level view of fund flows.

observable_signals.signal: Account shows high inbound fan-in followed by rapid narrow outbound concentration.
Funds dwell at each hop for far less time than genuine balances do.
Accounts occupy a dense component with no organic bridging structure.
Transfer amounts and timings are more regular than genuine person-to-person traffic.
Participating accounts are young relative to the value they are moving.

mitigations: Score fund flows at the network level, not per account.
Treat short dwell time combined with high fan-in as a first-class risk signal.
Share topology-derived risk signals across institutions where the framework permits.
references: FATF - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Red Flag Indicators
RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls

F6-39.name: Shell merchant-of-record laundering
F6-39.actor: An operator controlling one or more merchant accounts used to accept attacker-directed volume and convert it into clean settlement.
